question: A positive hydrostatic test (docimasia pulmonum) — where lung tissue floats in water — conclusively establishes that a neonate was born alive and breathed independently after delivery.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect. The hydrostatic test is not conclusive. False positives occur in putrefied specimens where decomposition gases inflate lung tissue. A positive test indicates air in lungs but cannot distinguish between air from breathing and gas from putrefaction. Always interpret alongside other signs of live birth and post-mortem findings.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this is false. The hydrostatic test has significant limitations: a positive result (floating) can occur due to putrefaction (gas in lungs from decomposition) — not only from air entry from breathing. A negative result (sinking) suggests the neonate did not breathe but does not exclude a live birth where the neonate briefly attempted breathing. The test is supportive evidence, not conclusive proof of live birth.
